editorNote: Extra Edition: IBM has opened the next chapter of the personal-computer race with a faster 80286 machine, larger disks, and room to grow.
morningLine: The AT arrives, adventures keep adults up late, and 1200-baud life gathers speed.

lead.headline: IBM's PC/AT Opens a Second Generation of Personal Computing
lead.dek: IBM unveils the 80286-powered 5170 with a 16-bit expansion path, high-capacity floppy, larger hard disks, and prices starting at $3,995.
body: IBM used August 14 to introduce two models of the Personal Computer AT, a machine it says runs more than twice as fast as the current PC family. Both are built around Intel's 80286, with a 24-bit address path and a 16-bit data path that moves the IBM line decisively beyond the original 8088 generation.

The $3,995 Model 68 carries 256KB of memory and a 1.2MB 5.25-inch diskette drive. The $5,795 Model 99 raises memory to 512KB, adds a 20MB fixed disk, and includes a serial-and-parallel adapter—figures that put serious business storage on the desktop at a serious business price.

Inside, eight expansion slots leave room for ambitious installations; six accept either new 16-bit or familiar 8-bit cards. A socket awaits the 80287 mathematics coprocessor, while IBM says memory can reach 3MB and direct-access storage 41.2MB.

The announcement reaches beyond hardware. DOS 3.0 supports the new disk formats, PC/IX support is promised later this year, and XENIX protected-mode support is due early in 1985. IBM also introduced networking pieces designed to make its growing PC family work together.

Analysts immediately called the AT the first model of a second generation of personal computers. Its reach may extend past Apple and other desktop rivals toward the multiuser systems sold by established minicomputer companies.

stories.headline: DOS 3.0 and PC Network Prepare IBM Machines to Share
body: DOS 3.0 is the quiet partner in IBM's loud hardware debut. It gives the AT command of the 20MB fixed disk and the new 1.2MB high-capacity floppy while retaining the ability to read several older PC diskette formats.

IBM also announced a PC Network adapter, cabling, and a translator unit. The company expects a network and operating system in early 1985 capable of linking as many as 72 users in standard configurations, pushing the personal computer deeper into shared office work.

stories.headline: Home-Computer Adventures Hook a Growing Adult Audience
body: Computer adventures are becoming an after-hours obsession for adults as well as a youthful pastime. A period wire feature finds players giving up sleep to wizards, priests, puzzles, and elaborate imaginary worlds.

The August shelves strengthen the spell. The Seven Cities of Gold and Boulder Dash headline Commodore 64 coverage, while arcade-flavored conversions and new quests crowd the listings. The attraction is not merely reflex: exploration, mapping, and problem solving can turn a short session into a long night.

worldAnchor.headline: Egyptian officials suspect Iran and Libya in mysterious Red Sea mining
worldAnchor.summary: A dated UPI report on August 13 said Egypt regarded Iran and Libya as prime suspects in mines that damaged shipping in the Red Sea, an important regional-security anchor.

bbsNote.headline: At 1200 Baud, Online Life Moves Beyond the Hobbyist Fringe
bbsNote.summary: August 1984 user-group coverage documented Timex/Sinclair owners connecting by modem to CompuServe, while the $699 Hayes Smartmodem 1200 represented the premium auto-dial/auto-answer standard. Period practice centered on terminal software, local BBS calls, downloads, and special-interest groups.

posts.text: An August 1984 CATS newsletter article by Mark Fendrick specifically covered modems and CompuServe for Timex/Sinclair users.
A period review listed the Hayes Smartmodem 1200 at $699, showing the price premium for faster, command-driven telecommunications.
A July 1984 Timelinez item announced a Bay Area Timex/Sinclair modem-owner directory with 13 members, illustrating how local user groups organized dial-up communities.

curiosity.headline: IBM's New Computer Came With a Two-Hour Tour on a Floppy
curiosity.summary: Every PC/AT shipped with Exploring the IBM Personal Computer AT, a self-loading tutorial disk available in monochrome and color versions.
curiosity.detail: IBM said the guided introduction took 1.5 to 2.5 hours and taught the keyboard, printer, disk storage, DOS, and text editing—an unusually elaborate out-of-box lesson for a professional machine.

gadgetWatch.headline: Compact Disc players push 'laser and computer' audio
gadgetWatch.summary: An August 1984 Technics SL-P8 advertisement sold the emerging CD format as a union of lasers and computers promising lifelike reproduction.

milestone.title: IBM introduces the PC/AT
milestone.note: The 80286-based AT and its 16-bit expansion architecture set the dominant high-end IBM-compatible PC template and marked the industry's transition beyond the original 8088 PC generation.
